title: Feeding Post-Newtonian Terms to a Neural Network Cuts Training Data by 10,000x
dek: A purely neural waveform model needs 10^8 to 10^10 training waveforms, but writing known physics into the network and letting it learn only the corrections needs just 8 numerical-relativity waveforms.
why: The first half covers the state of the field in gravitational-wave modeling; the second half, on surrogate speedups and the concrete numbers behind the PINN, is more worth hearing.
who: Graduate students and engineers working on gravitational-wave data analysis, numerical relativity, or scientific machine learning, especially those who want to use physics constraints to cut training-data requirements.
skip: The first ~5 minutes of conference introductions and detector-sensitivity-curve background can be fast-forwarded.

points.h: LIGO's error bars may come from theory, not the instrument
points.body: The speaker says that for some LIGO events, it cannot be ruled out that the analysis result is limited by understanding of waveform systematic errors, not just cryogenic cooling or mirror defects. GW23123 is an example: run different models and the posterior distributions show non-trivial differences. His position is not to take sides on who is right, but to give the models better error bars so the data analysts can keep arguing about who is right.

points.h: Double the simulation length, quadruple the error
points.body: The mismatch of numerical-relativity simulations scales roughly as the square of the wavelength. Because simulation accuracy is dominated by phase error, phase error accumulates linearly in time, and mismatch is the square of phase error. So wanting a simulation twice as long does not just mean waiting longer; you also have to make the accuracy higher, and the cost is penalized multiplicatively. Most simulations currently land at about 30 orbits, while the reference line is about 25 orbits.

points.h: For next-generation detectors, pure numerical relativity has no hope
points.body: The speaker showed a plot: the horizontal axis is event signal-to-noise ratio, the vertical axis is the number of simulations in the catalog with sufficient accuracy and length. For LIGO, about 85% to 90% of the catalog is sufficient, about 3000 simulations; but for heavy systems at 10^4 signal-to-noise ratio, only about 10 simulations in total are sufficient. For Cosmic Explorer and Einstein Telescope, the conclusion is that numerical relativity alone is completely insufficient and other models are needed to fill in.

points.h: Hybrid waveforms are actually stitching together two different physical systems
points.body: When splicing post-Newtonian waveforms with numerical-relativity waveforms, the cost function has many local minima in parameter space, and the global minimum falls in a narrow, shallow valley that optimizers struggle to find. The test is to run a simulation of about 60 orbits, then move the matching window and see what the early waveform looks like. The result is that the early numerical-relativity waveform and the post-Newtonian waveform look completely different, which amounts to smoothly stitching together waveforms from two different physical systems and introducing bias.

points.h: Let the neural network learn only what post-Newtonian cannot compute
points.body: Each additional post-Newtonian term is a PhD thesis worth of work, so the speaker's idea is to treat the neural network as encoding all the post-Newtonian terms he does not want to write by hand. The network needs only about 100 parameters, about 120 CPU hours of training, and only 8 numerical-relativity waveforms in mass-ratio space. Besides the waveform difference, the loss function also requires the orbital velocity to be close, the correction term to vanish as the orbital velocity goes to zero, and equal-mass symmetry and weight regularization.

points.h: Physics-informed networks extrapolate better outside the training set
points.body: At a point outside the training set, mass ratio 9 to 5, post-Newtonian completely fails near merger, the surrogate model (trained to mass ratio 8) has growing extrapolation error, while the physics-informed neural network performs much better. If after training to mass ratio 8 you add one data point at mass ratio 15, the error all the way to mass ratio 15 drops substantially. This promises to reduce the amount of training data needed to build models.

points.h: Purely neural approaches need more than 10,000 times the training data
points.body: The speaker says that most other attempts he has seen at modeling waveforms with neural networks throw physics away entirely and use only neural networks or autoencoders; that really requires 10^8 to 10^10 waveforms to train, meaning you would first have to build a surrogate to generate the training data, because it is impossible to obtain that many numerical-relativity waveforms. His conclusion: machine learning is a useful tool, but do not forget that you actually do know something about the thing you are modeling.

points.h: The surrogate's 30x to 40x speedup comes from changing the algorithm
points.body: The speaker says all he did was make the code less bad, with no revolutionary insight. The starting point was about 30 milliseconds, and now there is about a 30x to 40x speedup. The biggest speedup came from changing the algorithm: from cubic interpolation to tenth-order Hermite polynomials, with far fewer time nodes. Currently the dynamics part is the bulk, about 370 microseconds, while waveform evaluation takes only 50 microseconds. He estimates that eventually a frequency-domain waveform can be produced in 0.2 milliseconds, comparable to or better than the fastest phenom waveforms.

terms.def: A fast model that interpolates waveforms at arbitrary parameters from a small number of numerical-relativity simulations.
A network that writes known physics equations into its structure and lets the network learn only the correction terms.

A metric measuring the difference between two waveforms, dominated by phase error in numerical relativity.
A reference frame that rotates with the binary, making the waveform smoother and easier to model.
